title: Rumba names, composers and the dances behind them
summary: He names guaguanco composers, explains yuca and malanga rumba names, and says Cuban numbers always came with a dance, unlike bossa nova.

blocks.x: Okay. Do you know the names of the rumbas?

Yes. Guaguanco, 'El Guaguanco Es Lo Mas Sublime que Cubita Creo,' that was written by Ignacio Pineiro, that now if he was alive he was about 105 years old, and Cotinzen, from another neighborhood, and Malanga - he was a good rumbero and a good composer - Roncona, he was a good composer too, and there was a numerous composers.
So all the popular Cuban rhythms today, what they call Salsa today, were taken from this cult music in Cuba I see.

Create by the Creole because the religious part we never used it, we never used the religious part because we respect, we was so close, because my grandmother was African and the other mother, so we just can't play around with the religion.
Okay. So the rumbas - El Palo, La Yuca, El Guaguanco and the rumba all came from this music.

El Palo is a - is a - is another religion that we say is not is not a Christian religion. Is something to ah, to ah, to do a lot of a lot of things; Voodoo is a Voodoo so Malanga and Yuca that was the name they did because that was the the what we eat, the yuca, malanga, you

know, they are like potatoes, so they used to name what we actually like to eat, like yuca, malanga, name, so you know how they apply such a number to a rumba - now they say yuca - so they use to create because the most popular thing that what happened in Cuba is that everytime that we created a type of number, we created a dance for. That's why it became popular.

That happened with Bossa Nova here. There was no dance and the people like to listen to a Bossa Nova, it is a beautiful thing, but it was no dance for that. It was not like a Samba and march and and whatever.
